public_rationale: On February 26, 2025, Salesforce's CEO linked a plan to hire no new engineers that year to reported coding-tool productivity gains [e1]. This was a company statement, without an entry-level breakdown or independent verification of substitution [e1]. A research account published February 5, 2024 reported a 20% decline in freelance coding postings [e3]. The May 2025 Danish study found no significant earnings or recorded-hours effects across 11 exposed occupations, using outcomes through June 2024 [e2]. These findings do not establish complete engineering-role replacement or attribute entry-level engineering displacement to AI while addressing alternative causes [e1, e2, e3]. They also cannot establish that no qualifying public evidence existed by June 16, 2025, leaving the claim unresolved [e1, e2, e3].
limitations: The packet does not comprehensively establish what evidence was publicly available by June 16, 2025.
The evidence does not directly test whether coding automation can replace a complete engineering role [e1, e2, e3].
Hiring plans and freelance postings do not establish realized entry-level engineering job losses [e1, e3].
The Danish results cover outcomes through June 2024 and do not establish effects elsewhere or specifically among entry-level engineers [e2].

public_payload.normalized_proposition: You cannot just replace a coder because coding isn't really the job, and while this might affect entry-level software engineers at some point, there is yet to be proof it is happening or that AI rather than, say, outsourcing is taking these jobs.
conditions: this might affect entry-level software engineers at some point

statement.excerpt: You cannot just “replace a coder,” because “coder” isn’t really the job

our_interpretation: This concerns the public evidence available by publication, rather than a prediction that displacement can never occur.
Cannot just replace a coder is read as a claim about replacing an engineering role through coding automation alone, not a literal denial that coding occupations exist.
Proof means credible evidence connecting lost engineering work or positions to AI while addressing plausible alternative causes.
The target is the accumulated public record through June 16, 2025. Its start is unspecified because yet imposes a cutoff rather than a particular reporting year.
The possibility of future effects is a qualification, not a conditional forecast to score separately.
criteria.support_condition: A sufficiently comprehensive contemporaneous record supports the distinction between code generation and full engineering-role replacement, and establishes that claimed entry-level displacement had not been credibly attributed to AI rather than alternative causes.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence public by the post verifies replacement of complete engineering roles by AI, or credibly attributes entry-level engineering job losses or reduced hiring to AI while addressing relevant alternatives.

evidence.locator: Marc Benioff's response about workforce efficiency, near character 57083
evidence.publisher: Salesforce; transcript by S&P Global Market Intelligence
evidence.explanation: Benioff connects this hiring plan to reported gains from coding tools in the surrounding passage. It is material evidence of intended labor-demand substitution, but not verification of entry-level job losses or replacement of complete engineering roles.

The original Danish study reports small measured labor-market effects using administrative outcomes through June 2024, but cannot establish absence of displacement elsewhere or specifically among junior engineers. The source gives May 2025 only; available_at conservatively uses month-end.

evidence.locator: What will the future impact of generative AI be?
evidence.publisher: Imperial College Business School; Xinrong Zhu
evidence.explanation: The researcher reports declining freelance coding demand and comparisons between occupations with different AI exposure. This is substantive counterevidence to a broad denial of labor-demand effects, but the study does not identify entry-level engineering employees or demonstrate complete role replacement.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Evidence public by June 16, 2025 that verifies complete engineering-role replacement, or credibly attributes entry-level engineering job losses or reduced hiring to AI while addressing outsourcing and other plausible causes, would contradict the claim. Support would require a sufficiently comprehensive contemporaneous record establishing both the distinction between coding automation and full-role replacement and the absence of credible attribution of entry-level displacement to AI.
